name: Hydroxycitric acid
short: Garcinia supplements (hydroxycitric acid source): 2025 review, 34 liver-injury case reports, 1 death, 9 transplants, 1 confirmed by rechallenge. 2012 review: no report of direct harm from the acid.
text: The evidence of serious harm concerns weight-loss supplements made from Garcinia fruit (Garcinia cambogia, also called Garcinia gummi-gutta), whose active constituent is hydroxycitric acid, rather than purified hydroxycitric acid. A 2025 review of adverse-event databases and published reports identified more than 200 adverse events of liver injury from Garcinia consumption; 34 case reports included one death and nine liver transplants, 17 cases had causality scores indicating possible to highly probable causation by Garcinia supplements, and in one case causality was confirmed by rechallenge; among the proposed mechanisms the review lists liver-cell death caused by hydroxycitric acid. A 2022 letter reviewing the literature notes reported cases of acute liver injury from food supplements containing Garcinia cambogia and hydroxycitric acid, and European alerts from 2009 to 2021, and says that in some cases a relationship between hydroxycitric acid and liver toxicity was demonstrated. Two older reviews, both from 2012 and so earlier than the 2025 review, are more reassuring: one said that, at the doses usually given, no differences in side effects or adverse events (of those studied) had been reported in humans between people taking Garcinia cambogia extracts and controls, and the other said that the products reported to have adverse effects were polyherbal or multi-component and that, to that date, no case study or report had shown a direct adverse effect of hydroxycitric acid itself, although that review also mentions a few clinical toxicity reports of potential toxicity to sperm production with weight-loss supplements, some of them combinations including Garcinia or hydroxycitric acid. A meta-analysis of randomised weight-loss trials noted that gastrointestinal adverse events were twice as common with hydroxycitric acid as with placebo in one included study. In subchronic animal studies, high doses of certain hydroxycitric acid preparations caused testicular atrophy and impaired spermatogenesis, and a 2017 review concluded that, without adequate human data, particularly on the male reproductive system, substantial uncertainties exist about the safety of supplements containing high amounts of hydroxycitric acid. No interaction data were found in the cited sources.
